title: Paraphimosis and catheter emergencies
subtitle: Traumatic catheterisation, stuck balloons, urethral injury

sources.org: European Association of Urology (EAU) and European Society for Paediatric Urology (ESPU)
sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology: phimosis and paraphimosis
EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma: urethral trauma
Evidence-based guidelines for best practice in urological health care: catheterisation, indwelling catheters in adults, urethral and suprapubic
British Association of Urological Surgeons' suprapubic catheter practice guidelines (Harrison SCW et al., BJU International)

red_flags.text: A swollen, painful glans with a tight band of retracted foreskin behind it, often in a catheterised or confused patient whose foreskin was not replaced: paraphimosis.
Pain, bleeding and no urine flow after a catheter balloon is inflated: the balloon is in the urethra.
Blood at the meatus, inability to void, or a perineal or penile 'butterfly' haematoma after pelvic fracture or straddle injury: urethral injury.
A catheter balloon that will not deflate, or a catheter that has fallen out of a recently formed suprapubic tract.
Fever and rigors after a difficult or traumatic catheterisation.

do_now.text: Paraphimosis: give analgesia or a penile block, reduce the oedema with sustained manual compression, then reduce the foreskin by pushing the glans back while drawing the foreskin forward.
If manual reduction fails, a dorsal slit under anaesthesia is required; do not leave a constricting band in place.

Balloon inflated in the urethra: deflate it immediately, remove the catheter, and do not reattempt blindly. Ask for urological help for a further attempt, ideally with a flexible cystoscope and guidewire.
Suspected urethral injury: do not attempt blind urethral catheterisation by an inexperienced operator. Divert the urine with a suprapubic catheter if the patient cannot void, and image the urethra.

Dislodged suprapubic catheter: replace it promptly through the existing tract, because a fresh tract can close within hours; a recently formed tract, in the first weeks after insertion, may need replacement by the urology team.

assess.text: Always replace the foreskin after catheterisation or examination, and document that you did so.
Before any catheter in trauma, examine the meatus, the perineum and, where indicated, the rectum.
Sepsis screen after a traumatic catheterisation in infected urine.

investigate.text: Retrograde urethrography when urethral injury is suspected, in a stable patient, before further attempts at urethral catheterisation.
Bladder ultrasound to confirm retention or a full bladder before suprapubic access.
Ultrasound to see a balloon that will not deflate, and to guide its puncture.

resuscitate.text: Treat urosepsis after traumatic catheterisation with antibiotics per local protocol once cultures are sent.

definitive.text: Paraphimosis: after reduction, arrange elective circumcision discussion for recurrent or underlying phimosis.
False passage: a urethral catheter passed by a urologist under direct vision is left for a period to allow healing; otherwise a suprapubic catheter.

Non-deflating balloon: cut the inflation valve arm first; if that fails, pass a fine guidewire up the inflation channel, or puncture the balloon under ultrasound guidance. Retrieve and inspect the balloon fragments.
Pelvic fracture urethral injury: suprapubic diversion, with primary realignment in selected cases and delayed urethroplasty for the resulting stricture.

escalate.text: Urology registrar for any traumatic catheterisation, suspected urethral injury, or failed paraphimosis reduction.
Trauma team leader before catheterising any patient with a pelvic fracture.
Radiology for a balloon puncture under ultrasound guidance.

notes: Paraphimosis is iatrogenic far more often than it should be. The fix is a habit: the foreskin goes back over the glans every time.
Never over-inflate a balloon to burst it, and never inject solvents into it. Fragments are left behind and become bladder stones.

In a pelvic fracture, the first catheter attempt is the one that matters. A confident gentle attempt by an experienced urologist is very different from repeated attempts by the most junior person in the room.
